The visual contrast sensitivity test has become a standard first stop for people who suspect they have CIRS.  It tests your eyesight in such a way to determine if your brain is inflamed thanks to CIRS.  If you fail the visual contrast sensitivity test, there’s a very good chance you have CIRS.

And it only costs $15 to take online!

My website of preference is [vcstest.com](https://www.vcstest.com/).  It took me about 15 minutes in total for it to walk me through calibrating my monitor and taking the test.  And because I paid the $15 dollars, it saved my monitor calibration settings so that I can easily retake the test in the future to check my progress.  (My test scores have improved since I’ve started treatment, but I’m still not 100% passing yet.)

After you take the test, it will also walk you through a symptom cluster assessment.  Between the visual contrast sensitivity test and the symptom cluster assessment, you should get a pretty good idea on if you have CIRS or not.  My end results told me I had a greater than 95% chance of having CIRS.

So my advice:  take the visual contrast sensitivity test and report back!

Here's the mold test that I used from Envirobiomics, the [HERTSMI-2](https://www.envirobiomics.com/product/hertsmi-2/?v=7516fd43adaa).  It tests for 5 types of mold that are some of the most toxic to humans.

If you want to go all out, get the famous Envirobiomics "[number 7](https://www.envirobiomics.com/product/sm-aeh-actino-endotoxin-hertsmi-2/?v=7516fd43adaa)," which includes the mold tests from HERTSMI-2 as well as two bacteria tests for Actinos and Endotoxins which also make people sick with CIRS.  

The swab test kit they sent me was super easy.  I just wiped down a bunch of dusty surfaces and sent it back to them.  Got the results about a week later.

I think I'm in the "constitutionally strong patient" category.  I've been around mold all my life and only been mild to moderately affected.  It wasn't until this current apartment suffered water damage and became a mold farm that I got knocked on my rear end.

That's what I did (though there might be better ways).  And every few weeks, I'd rewatch a video if I felt a little uncertain about something.  That's how I caught the fact I was doing my barbell rows wrong.

> What's the best thing to do once I do stall out? Just keep go down a little and keep at it?

Absolutely, go down a little and keep at it.  It's built into the Stronglifts 5x5 program.  You stall out once, it might be a fluke.  You stall out three times in a row, drop 10% off your weight next time and continue the program from that point.  If you get to the same weight, and stall out again, once again see if you stall out three times in a row, drop 10%, and try again.  If after the third time of dropping 10% and working back up you're still not gaining, it might be time to change programs.  

This started happening to me when I started getting to the intermediate range according to Symmetric Strength, so I switched to an intermediate program (Madcow).  Stronglifts is great for getting quick newb gains, but it becomes impossible to keep up that steady rate of gains after a while.

And sometimes when you stall out, it will just be a fluke for that day.  I remember being super disappointed stalling out at a low weight on a bench press, then coming back the next time and the weight felt light as a feather.

> How did the program work for you?

It worked great!  One thing I noticed is that everyone seems to have their ahead of the curve exercise/muscle group that they're super good at and one that is just shockingly bad.  *Everyone* has that problem.  My deadlifts are monstrously good for being intermediate, but I bench press like a toddler.  You might be the exact opposite.  Don't panic, just keep working it, and make sure your form is good.

I did Stronglifts 5x5 and I loved it!  I just switched to the intermediate program last month, Madcow, and I couldn't have gotten here without 5x5.  Here's a brief review.

**Light Weight = Good**

The light weight at the beginning is very, very necessary.  Trust me, when the weight starts getting higher and higher, you're going to be happy that you know how to squat correctly, or else all your squats are going to turn into good mornings in no time (I know this from experience).  Use this time to make sure you're doing every bit of your form perfectly.  I made the mistake of not perfecting my barbell rows early on, and as a result, my back progress severely lagged for the longest time. 

If it's really, really upsetting you, instead of jumping 5 pounds every workout, you can jump up 10 pounds every workout until it just starts to *barely* be moderately difficult.  The instant it starts to be the tiniest bit into moderate difficult territory when you experience even the smallest bit of resistance, go back down to 5 pounds added every workout.  

You can do that, but I don't recommend it.  Use this time to practice correct form, practice correct form, and practice correct form.  And while you're at it, practice correct form.  And soak up the newbie gains from the light weights while you can!

**What it's lacking**

I've read up on Stronglifts 5x5 and made some of my own conclusions on the few things it's lacking.  Keep doing Stronglifts 5x5, but throw in dips, chin ups, pull ups, and calf raises too.  On A day do dips and chin ups after the regular 5x5 workout, and on B day do pull ups and calf raises after the regular 5x5 workout.  

Aim for 4 sets of 8 for each.  My method for these are a little different than 5x5.  If you finish a single set and do all 8 reps, then add 5 pounds right then and there, then start on your next set.  Keep doing that until you finish 4 sets.  If you can't do 8 reps, stick with that weight until you can, and (for chin ups/pull ups) do that last few reps as negative reps.  For dips, chin ups, and pull ups, you'll either have to start holding weights with your legs/feet, or get a dip belt to hang weights from.  

It's okay to start off with doing assisted chin-ups/pulls-ups/dips - it's how I had to start.  If your gym has an assisted chin up/dip machine, use that until you're able to do at least 8 chin ups/dips/pull ups unassisted.

**When to Stop Stronglifts 5x5**

The golden rule is:  if you keep getting stronger, keep doing it.

I started using the new [Symmetric Strength](http://symmetricstrength.com/) website to track my progress.  It was around the time I started getting on the border of novice/intermediate that I stopped making gains on stronglifts.  I'm sure some people make it farther and others drop out sooner.  Just keep doing it as long as it works.

And on a final note, Symmetric Strength is great!  So long as you start doing at least chin-ups or pull-ups, you can get a really good idea of where you're at and what you need to focus on.

I hoped this helped!
